transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Well, I guess I'm here because lately I just feel like I really don't deserve the trust people put in me. I work as a doctor, and I just keep replaying these small clinical imperfections in my head over and over. It's gotten to the point where I feel like those little things prove I'm a dangerous doctor. It's just been weighing on me a lot, and I thought I should talk to someone about it.

When you replay these clinical imperfections in your head, do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly to try to manage or reduce the anxiety—like checking records, seeking reassurance from colleagues, or anything like that?

No, not really. I don't go back and check patient charts over and over, or anything like that. And I definitely don't ask my colleagues for reassurance... honestly, I think I'd be too ashamed to bring it up to them anyway. 

It's more just something that stays in my head. I just sit there and dwell on how I handled a case, but I don't have any specific routines or habits I do to try and make the anxiety go away. I just kind of sit with the feeling.

When you think about these clinical imperfections, do you genuinely believe they represent real mistakes that could have harmed a patient, or do you recognize that these thoughts might be out of proportion to what actually happened?

I genuinely believe they are real mistakes. I mean, even when I review the chart and there is absolutely no evidence of a bad outcome, I just keep believing that some routine delay, or maybe an imperfect message from me, has quietly harmed a patient. I can't just brush it off as being out of proportion. I really believe that I've caused harm and that everyone is eventually going to discover it.
Even though you believe these mistakes have caused harm, do you ever have moments where you question whether your belief is actually true, or does it always feel completely real and certain to you?

No, I... I don't really have moments where I question it. It feels completely real to me all the time. 

Like I mentioned a minute ago, I can look right at the chart, see that there's no evidence of a bad outcome, and it just doesn't matter. I still firmly believe that a routine delay or some imperfect message I left has quietly harmed them. The certainty doesn't go away. It's not a "maybe" in my head. I just know it happened, and I'm just waiting for the day everyone discovers what I did.
Apart from these thoughts about harming patients, have you ever experienced things like hearing voices that others couldn't hear, or seeing things that weren't there?

Yes, I have. Sometimes when I’m alone after clinic, or when I'm just trying to fall asleep... I hear a patient’s voice. It sounds as clearly as if they were standing right there in the room with me, just saying, "You missed it." 

It sounds so real that I'll actually get up and check the hallway, or I'll look at my phone, even though nothing is there. I haven't really seen things that weren't there, but I definitely hear that voice.

When you hear that patient's voice saying 'You missed it,' does it feel like it's directly commenting on or confirming your belief that you've harmed a patient, or does it feel more like a random voice that's separate from those thoughts?

It definitely feels connected. It's like... it's confirming exactly what I'm already thinking. It's not just some random voice. It ties right into that feeling that I've messed up and hurt someone. 

And, you know, it's strange because... before all this started, before I got that clinic award and this whole low period began, I never experienced anything like this. I never heard voices, and I was never convinced I was secretly harming people when the charts said otherwise. It’s like these voices and this... this absolute certainty that I'm guilty... they only happen now, when I'm stuck in this really low state.

Before this current low period that started after not getting the clinic award, have you ever experienced a time lasting at least two weeks where you felt persistently depressed or lost interest in things you normally enjoyed?

No, I haven't. Before this whole thing started a few months ago, I never really had a period like that. I mean, sure, residency was stressful and there were tough weeks, but nothing like this. I never felt this persistently down or completely lost interest in everything for weeks on end. This is the first time I've ever experienced anything like this.
